- the oracle holds.

**Keys Mandu found keeps the focus (2026-10-11).** In Rules' *Keys Mandu
found* (§4.25r) each row has a tick box and a ⋯. The ⋯ opens the row to
*Show in policy.yaml* and *Not a secret*, and **Scan for keys** heads the
card. `home.js renderSuggested` draws the list again from nothing for every
tick and every ⋯, and for each changed read of the 3-second poll while a
scan runs. Until 2026-10-11, in headless Chromium:

- Enter on a row's ⋯ (open or close), and Space on its tick box, left the
  focus on `<body>`, at the top of the page;
- *Not a secret* goes off during its POST, and Chromium drops the focus of
  a button turned off. The row is then gone;
- *Scan for keys* goes off for the whole scan and came back on with no
  focus. A tick or a ⋯ during its POST, which waits up to 20 s, turned it
  back on from the last listing, mid-scan;
- *Show in policy.yaml* and *Not a secret* named no row. *Show* kept its
  words while the lines showed.

Now:

- **A tick, a ⋯, the poll.** `renderSuggested` takes the focus's place in
  the list before it draws, as the poll takes it (`pollPlace`). After the
  draw, only if the focus fell, it gives it back (`pollRefocus`). A row is
  found by its `data-id` and `data-path`, then its tick box or ⋯ by rank in
  the row, so an opened row above it moves nothing. A control gone from its
  place gives the focus to the card's heading. The scan line is drawn
  after, so a scan that ends on the same redraw never takes a focus the
  list gives back.
- **Not a secret.** The place is taken before the button goes off:
  - when it works, the row is gone and the focus goes to the card's
    heading, *Keys Mandu found*, as *Your rules*' Remove goes to its own;
  - when it is refused, the focus goes back to the button, on again. The
    button is then described by the card's error line
    (`aria-describedby="suggest-error"`).
- **Show in policy.yaml** reads *Hide policy.yaml* while the lines show, as
  in *Your rules* (`sourceWords`). The lines stay shown through a redraw
  (`G.yaml`), so the button keeps its words and the focus finds it again.
  Opening another row shows that row's lines closed.
- **Scan for keys** stays off while its own POST is on its way (`G.posting`),
  whatever draws the list meanwhile. It is described by the error line, so
  a refusal is read with it. On again, after a refusal or when the scan
  ends (its POST, or the poll), it gets the focus back if it had it when it
  went off, the focus fell meanwhile, and the card is still open
  (`scanButtonOff`). A refusal that needs a folder still gives the focus to
  the folder box. While it is off, its focus waits on the card's heading
  (since 2026-10-13, *While a scan runs, the focus waits on the heading*,
  below).
- **The names.** Each opened-row button names its row by the row's own
  name, its words first: "Show in policy.yaml: staging.conf" (then "Hide
  policy.yaml: …") and "Not a secret: staging.conf". Only one row is open
  at a time, so no name is shared.
- **Nothing is taken.** A tick, a ⋯ or *Not a secret* pressed while the
  focus is elsewhere, or nowhere, moves nothing. A focus the person moves
  during a scan stays where they put it.

Sighted readers see one change: *Show in policy.yaml* reads *Hide
policy.yaml* while its lines show. Presentation only: no route, server text
or decision changed. **Not covered:**

- a row's tick box and ⋯ were named by the file's name alone ("Skip
  app.conf"), so two keys in files of the same name in different folders
  shared their names: now named apart, *Keys in files of the same name are
  named apart*, below;
- while a scan runs, the focus of a pressed *Scan for keys* stayed on
  `<body>` (the button is off), and the status line says what runs: now it
  waits on the card's heading, *While a scan runs, the focus waits on the
  heading*, below.

Tests: `home-js-suggested-focus.test.ts` (jsdom; `press` drops the focus of
the button turned off, as Chromium does) covers:

- the ⋯ opened and closed, also with another row open above it;
- the tick box, unticked and ticked again;
- *Show* / *Hide* with the lines kept through a redraw;
- *Not a secret*, done and refused;
- *Scan for keys* kept off through its POST despite a tick, then the focus
  back when the scan ends: with its answer, or with the poll after a
  refocused tick box, which keeps the focus;
- a refused scan, and one that needs a folder;
- a scan that ends after the card was closed, which focuses nothing hidden;
- nothing taken;
- the names, with no name shared.

Nineteen mutations of the change are each caught. Stack
`tests/stack/suggested-focus.test.ts` uses a real arbiter with an empty
policy.yaml and a work tree holding three keys the real workspace scan
files, and a real dashboard over the production adapter serving Rules:

- signed in, ⋯, a tick and *Show in policy.yaml* keep their focus;
- *Not a secret* goes to the heading, and the arbiter no longer lists the
  key;
- *Scan for keys* gets the focus back, and its line counts the key marked
  as not a secret;
- signed out on the open page (a session that ended), a refused *Not a
  secret* and a refused Scan keep their focus, described by "Sign in
  first…", and nothing changes;
- the oracle holds: no key, nor an 8-character run of one, in a page or an
  answer.

**While a scan runs, the focus waits on the heading (2026-10-13).** A scan
takes from a second to a minute: its POST waits up to 20 s, and the 3 s
poll follows a scan still running after it. *Scan for keys* is off all that
time, so until 2026-10-13 the focus of a person who pressed it sat on
`<body>` for the whole scan, and the next Tab started at the top of the
page. Now:

- **The heading holds it.** Before the button goes off with the focus on
  it (`scanButtonOff`: its own press, or a scan another tab started that
  the poll reads), the focus moves to the card's heading, *Keys Mandu
  found* (`focusThere`, no Tab stop, no ring), as Send's waits on the
  preview's headline (§4.25t). The line beside the button, `role="status"`,
  says what runs; the focus is not put on that line, as a live region that
  takes the focus may be read twice.
- **It comes back.** When the button is on again (the scan ended, with its
  answer or the poll, or was refused), it gets the focus back if the focus
  still waits on the heading, or fell meanwhile (a click on nothing), and
  the card is open. A closed card leaves it on the heading, which a closed
  card still shows. A refusal that needs a folder gives it to the folder
  box, as before.
- **A focus the person moves stays.** A move from the heading to another
  place on the page (a `focusout` with a `relatedTarget`) ends the wait:
  the end of the scan then takes nothing, also when something brings the
  focus back to the heading meanwhile (*Not a secret* done). Enter in the
  folder box starts the scan with the focus kept in the box, before and
  after.

Sighted readers see no change. Presentation only: no route, server text or
decision changed. Rejected: keeping the button focusable with
`aria-disabled`, which leaves a submit button that a second Enter would
press. Tests: in `home-js-suggested-focus.test.ts`, `pressOff` drops the
focus only while the button still has it, as Chromium does. Its scan cases
cover the heading through the POST, a redraw and the poll, then *Scan for
keys* again, which a later redraw then leaves alone; a focus moved into
the list; a focus that fell; the folder box; a scan another tab started; a
closed card; and both refusals. Seven of them fail on the old page; the
other two are guards. Thirteen of fifteen mutations of the change are each
caught; the other two change nothing a page can see (the wait is never on
while the focus is anywhere but the heading or nowhere, and a listener left
behind only clears a flag already clear). Stack
`tests/stack/suggested-focus.test.ts` K4 and K5 check the heading right
after the press, over the real scan, and *Scan for keys* again after it.

**Keys in files of the same name are named apart (2026-10-11).** Each row
of *Keys Mandu found* is named by its file's name (`s.name`, the path's
base name; "1 old version of config.py" for old versions), and until
2026-10-11 every control and sentence about the row used that name alone.
A project with `services/api/app.conf` and `services/web/app.conf`, or two
`config.py`, the common shape of a project of several services, gave two
tick boxes read "Save app.conf", two ⋯ "More about app.conf", two Skips in
*Changes to save* "Skip the suggestion for app.conf", and a *Not a secret*
that asked "Mark app.conf as not a secret?" and then said "app.conf is
marked as not a secret" of either file. Now `home.js suggestionName`:

- **A name of its own stays.** A row whose name no other suggestion has is
  named as before: "Save ci.conf".
- **A shared name gives way to the path.** Where another suggestion has the
  same name, the row is named by its path (`s.display`, `~`-shortened):
  "Save ~/proj/services/web/app.conf", "More about …", "About …" (the
  opened row), "Show in policy.yaml: …" / "Hide policy.yaml: …", "Not a
  secret: …", and "Skip the suggestion for …" in *Changes to save*. Old
  versions name their file's path: "1 old version of
  ~/proj/services/web/config.py".
- **Not a secret says which file.** Its question and its notice use the
  same words, taken before the request, so the notice names the file
  marked even though the other one has its name to itself afterwards.

The names follow the list: a scan that files a second `app.conf` names the
first by its path too, and one marked as not a secret gives the other its
short name back. The focus is unaffected (`pollRefocus` finds a control by
its place and its visible words, not its name). Sighted readers see the
same rows; only the question and the notice show the path when two names
clash. Presentation only: no route, server text or decision changed. **Not
covered:** two suggestions on one path (a scan's and a model's) would
still share a name.

Tests: `home-js-suggested-names.test.ts` (jsdom, the server's own rows)
covers the tick boxes, the ⋯ and *Changes to save*'s Skips of two
`app.conf` and a lone `ci.conf` with no name shared; the opened row's
label, *Show* / *Hide* and *Not a secret*; *Not a secret*'s question and
notice, after which the other `app.conf` has its short name again; a lone
file's words unchanged; and old versions under two `config.py`. Four of its
five cases fail on the old page (the fifth is a guard), and eleven
mutations of the change are each caught. Stack
`tests/stack/suggested-names.test.ts` uses a real arbiter with an empty
policy.yaml and a work tree holding keys in `services/api/app.conf`,
`services/web/app.conf` and `tools/ci.conf`, which the real workspace scan
files, and a real dashboard over the production adapter serving Rules,
signed in:

- each control names its row apart, and no two share a name;
- the web `app.conf`'s opened row names its path, and its policy.yaml lines
  are that file's;
- *Not a secret* asks and tells of that path, and the arbiter lists the
  other `app.conf` still;
- the oracle holds.

**A box that scrolls says what it holds (2026-10-12).** Chromium (since
130, as Firefox) makes a box that overflows and holds nothing to focus a
Tab stop of its own, so a keyboard can scroll it, and a screen reader reads
that stop by its role and name. Until 2026-10-12 none of the product page's
had a name. In a headless Chromium the model preview's list of 55 file
and folder names, focused, was a list named by every name in it run together, and a
suggestion's policy.yaml lines a `generic` named by all their text. Now each
such box has a role (a list keeps its own; a `<pre>` is a `group`, since
ARIA 1.2 forbids naming a generic, as with the cards in *A question has a
name*) and a name made of its own words:

| Box (app.css) | Where | Name |
|---|---|---|
| `#suggest-model-list` | *Ask a model too*'s preview | its caption's words ("The names it sends, exactly as sent"), as `aria-label`: the caption is drawn in capitals, which a browser puts in a name taken from it |
| `pre.suggestion-yaml` | an opened suggestion | the words above it, "Save adds these lines to policy.yaml:" (`nameBy`) |
| `#files-impact` | *Changes to save* | "What this changes" |
| `#files-confirm-list` | the weaker-change question | its bold words, "These changes make protection weaker." |
| `.files-confirm-files ul` | the same | the words above it, "Files that become less protected:" |
| `pre.code-block` | a fenced block in a reply or your prompt | "Code" |
| `pre.hidden-text` | *Show what was hidden*, *Show the real value* | "What was hidden"; "The real value" (of NAME when an item holds several) |

A name is never what the box holds: the real value's box names the secret,
never the value. It is a `group`, not a `region`, because a page draws
several code blocks and revealed boxes, and landmarks of the same name are
a fault. No `tabindex` is added: the browser decides when a box is a stop
(a box that does not overflow is none). The other boxes that scroll (`#nav`,
`.files-list`, `.files-pending`, `.files-pending-list`) hold links or
buttons, so they are never a stop of their own. `.files-list` is a folder's
entries and *Keys Mandu found*'s list; *Your rules*' tree is no box at all
since 2026-10-14 (§4.25f *The tree is as long as its rules*). No
`aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` on the page points at an element
holding one of these boxes, so no other name changes. Sighted readers see no change.
Presentation only: no route, server text or CSS changed. The inspector's
session page follows the same rule (§4.32 *A box that scrolls says what it
holds*).

Tests: `home-js-scroll-names.test.ts` (jsdom with mandu.css and app.css
applied, so "may scroll" is the computed overflow; the sweep helpers
`scrollStops` / `scrollFaults` are in `control-names.ts`):

- every rule of the product styles that scrolls is listed as holding
  controls or as named, so a new one is a decision;
- the agent page's fenced block, What was hidden and the real value (one
  secret, and each of two), and the note under your message;
- the preview's list (an empty preview keeps no name), a suggestion's
  lines, and *Changes to save*'s box and its question's two lists;
- on each surface, every box that may scroll and holds nothing to focus has
  a role and a name.

Five of its six cases fail on the old page (the sweep is a guard). Stack
`tests/stack/scroll-names.test.ts` (secrets) serves the pages with the
served styles. On Rules, a real arbiter scans a work tree of 40 notes and a
key, and starts its fake classifier for a Names-only preview; a real
dashboard over the production adapter serves Rules signed in. The lines,
the list and the question's lists are named, and the classifier got no run.
On the agent page, the real anthropic-proxy carries a turn in which a
scripted model reads a `.env` and replies with a fenced block. The block is
named "Code", and the value shown on a click is in a box named "The real
value". The oracle: no key in the model's turns, the classifier's request,
or any page or answer but the value the person asked to see.

**A short question keeps its icon beside its words (2026-10-12).** Every
question card starts with one row: the family icon (40 px), then the words
(`.ask-body`, a 320 px flex basis), 20 px apart. The row wraps, so on a
phone the icon goes above the words. A browser sizes that row by its own
width before it lays it out: in a card that stacks its parts (`.ask.expanded`)
it is measured at fit-content, and on Home it takes its max-content width.
Both are the icon, the gap and the words' own width. Until 2026-10-12 a
sentence shorter than 320 px made the row narrower than the three, so it
was laid out wrapped. A headless Chromium at 1280 px drew Approvals'
"Your agent wants to change a rule" (every rule change your agent asked
for) and "Claude Code wants to run `curl`" with a 109 px header that held
49 px of content: the row was measured wrapped, then stretched to the card,
which left an empty band above and below the sentence. The agent page's
*Needs your OK* and the "Mandu found N possible keys" card drew the same.
On Home, whose cards carry the reason in the line under the sentence, a
short reason would put the icon above the words and float the buttons
mid-card. A long sentence never wrapped, so the tour's pictures are as
they were.

Now the row is one class, `.ask-top` (app.css), for all three cards that
draw an icon (`askCard`, `proposalCard`, the possible-keys card), in place
of two inline styles and `.suggestion-card-top`. Its `min-width:
min(100%, 380px)` is the icon, the gap and the words' basis, so the row is
never measured narrower than the two side by side, or the card where the
card is narrower. A one-line question's header is 49 px at 1280 and 760 px.
On a phone (a card under 380 px) every card is as before, with the icon
above the words. Presentation only: no route, question, answer, focus rule
or server text changed.

Tests: `home-js-ask-top.test.ts` (jsdom with mandu.css and app.css
applied):

- the stylesheet's arithmetic: `.ask-top`'s min-width is `.ask-icon`'s
  width, `.ask-top`'s gap and `.ask-body`'s basis, inside `min(100%, …)`;
  the possible-keys card has no rule of its own;
- Home's and Approvals' waiting cards (short and long), a rule change your
  agent asked for, the possible-keys card and the agent page's *Needs your
  OK*: each draws its icon in an `.ask-top` with no inline style that
  computes a wrapping flex row, the gap and the min-width.

All four cases fail on the old page, and 10 of 10 mutations are caught.
Stack `tests/stack/ask-top-row.test.ts` (secrets) serves Approvals and Home
with the served styles. A real arbiter holds the agent's binding of `.env`
to a host, which waits; the real scan files a key; and the real egress gate
asks about a masked variable. A real dashboard over the production adapter
serves the pages signed in. Each card's header is an `.ask-top` with the
min-width, and no page or answer read holds a secret's value. jsdom has no
layout, so the heights above are the Chromium probe's.

**A question's buttons wrap inside its card (2026-10-14).** Every card
that asks the person something ends in one row of answers, `.ask-actions`
(app.css): a wrapping flex row that never shrinks, so on Home's wide card
the words give way and the buttons stay on one line. Nothing bounded
the row, so it was always as wide as all its buttons on one line, and the
wrap it asks for never happened. On a phone the answers ran past the card. A
headless Chromium with the page's own styles measured how far the last
button ends past the card's content:

| Card | 320 px | 390 px | 760 px |
|---|---|---|---|
| A send (Allow once, Always allow, Block) | 70 px, *Block* cut at the screen's edge | 0 | 0 |
| A program's send (Allow once, Allow this session, Block) | 101 px | 31 px | 0 |
| A held message on Approvals (four answers) | 435 px | **365 px** | 24 px |
| A held message on Home (three answers) | 194 px | 124 px | 0 |

A held message (§4.34) on Approvals at 390 px made the whole page scroll
sideways to 714 px, with *Send masked*, the safe answer, off screen. No
survey had drawn one: the tour has only sends.

Now the row is never wider than its own row (`max-width: 100%`), so on a
phone the buttons wrap onto another line inside the card. It still never
shrinks, so on a wide card the words give way first. Measured again at 320,
360, 375, 390, 414, 760 and 1280 px, no button runs past its card and no
page scrolls sideways. At 1280 px every card is unchanged (same rows and
heights). At 390 px a send's card is unchanged (its three buttons fit),
and the held message's four answers take three lines. At 760 px only the
held message's card, which ran over, now takes two. The rule covers every card that uses the
row: Home's and Approvals' questions, the agent page's *Needs your OK*, a
rule change your agent asked for, the possible-keys card and a suggested
rule's *Discard* / *Apply*. Presentation only: no route, answer, focus rule
or server text changed.

Tests: `home-js-ask-actions.test.ts` (jsdom with mandu.css and app.css as a
390 px phone applies them):

- the stylesheet: `.ask-actions` wraps, never shrinks and has `max-width:
  100%`, and no phone rule takes the bound away. A sweep checks that no
  rule of the page both wraps its children and never shrinks without a
  `max-width`;
- every card listed above draws its answers in one `.ask-actions`, with no
  inline style, which computes that rule. The answers and their order are
  as before.

All seven cases fail on the old page, and 8 of 8 mutations are caught.
Stack `tests/stack/question-buttons-wrap.test.ts` (secrets) serves Home and
Approvals with the served styles at 390 px. A real arbiter has a prompt
pack whose codename the person set to ask. The real anthropic-proxy holds a
message that names it, and the real egress gate asks about a registered
`.env`'s key. A real dashboard over the production adapter serves both
pages signed out. Each card's row computes the rule: the held message has
its three answers on Home and its four on Approvals, and the send has its
three. No page or answer holds the key or the found text. jsdom has no
layout, so the widths above are the Chromium probe's.

The agent page's secret cards, which ran past a small phone, are the next
paragraph.

**A grid column is never wider than its box (2026-10-14).** A grid of
`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(320px, 1fr))` columns lays out as many 320 px or
wider columns as fit, but never makes one narrower than 320 px, even in a
narrower box. The agent page's *Your secrets* cards (`.secret-cards`,
app.css) were such a grid. A headless Chromium survey of both front-ends
at 320 px found this the only sideways page scroll left: each card was
320 px wide in its 288 px box (the page's 16 px gutters). It ran 16 px past
the screen, its right edge, level tag and *Show the real value* were cut
off, and the page scrolled sideways to 336 px. This held on every screen
narrower than 352 px (320 + 2 × 16). Everything else the survey found past
the edge sits in a scroller built for it: the nav rows, the session tabs
and the inspector's tables.

The inspector had the same pattern. The ▶ Run drills dialog's scenario
list (`.watch-scenarios`, §4.22) is a 340 px `auto-fill` column in a dialog
`min(880px, 94vw)` wide. A Chromium probe with the dialog's markup and
styles measured the column 340 px in a 265, 302 and 331 px box at 320, 360
and 390 px, so every row was cut (75, 38 and 9 px) and the list scrolled
sideways inside its box.

Now every `auto-fit` and `auto-fill` column whose minimum is a fixed
length is bounded by its box: `minmax(min(<length>, 100%), 1fr)`. That is
the same column wherever the box is at least that wide, and the box's
width where it is not. The bound goes on the two that ran over and on the
three that fit today (the agent page's facts tiles, 180 px; the inspector's
protection levels, `.prot-presets`, 200 px; *Test a flow*'s form, 180 px), so
a narrower box never cuts them either. Measured again at 320, 360, 390, 760
and 1280 px, the cards fill their box at 320 px and the page no longer
scrolls sideways. At 360 px and wider every grid has the same tracks and
the page the same height as before. The scenario list fits its box at
every width, and it is unchanged at 414 px and wider. Presentation only: no
route, word, focus rule or server text changed.

Tests: `css-grid-columns-fit.test.ts`:

- the three stylesheets (mandu.css, app.css, dev/dashboard.css, every
  `@media` block): no `auto-fit` or `auto-fill` column has a fixed minimum
  that its box does not bound, and each of the five keeps its own length;
- no script of either front-end draws a grid's columns inline, so the
  stylesheet decides for every grid the pages draw;
- the agent page in jsdom, with its styles as a 320 px phone applies them:
  the two cards and the facts' tiles compute the bound with no inline
  style;
- the inspector's index.html with its styles at 390 px: the scenario list
  computes it.

Four of the five cases fail on the old page (the script sweep is a guard).
Stack `tests/stack/secret-cards-fit.test.ts` (secrets) runs a real arbiter
with `.env` and `creds.json` at `no-model`, and the real anthropic-proxy
on its production client carrying a session whose scripted model reads
both. A real dashboard serves the agent page, which with its served styles
at 320 px draws the two cards and the tiles under the bound, signed in and
signed out. The served inspector's scenario list keeps its bound too.
Neither value reached the model, a drawn page or a signed-out answer. jsdom
has no layout, so the widths above are the Chromium probe's.

Not covered: a grid with fixed columns outside `repeat()` (for example the
rows' `180px minmax(0, 1fr) …`) relies on its own phone rule, and this
sweep does not read it.

A grid that declares no columns has one `auto` column, as wide as its
widest child's min-content, and this sweep does not read that either. The
inspector's trace was such a grid. It ran past a mid-width window, and
since 2026-10-15 it declares `minmax(0, 1fr)` (§4.33 *The trace and its
key fit a narrow column*).

**The page links fit a small phone (2026-10-15; app.css).** At 640 px and
narrower the four page links take a row of their own under the brand and
the status, as wide as the page's column (288 px at 320 px), and the row
scrolls sideways if they do not fit. The survey above counted that row
among the scrollers built for it. With nothing waiting the links needed
287 px at 320 px (288 on Approvals, where its word is 500), so they just
fit; the count's pill beside Approvals adds 29 px for one digit and 36 for
two. A headless Chromium over the served page, with one request waiting,
drew "Home · Approvals 1 · Rules · Settir" at 320 px. With anything
waiting, Settings ran past the row at 320 to 355 px on every page, and
nothing showed that the row scrolled. 320 px is also a 1280 px window at
400 % zoom.

Now, narrower than 375 px, the links sit closer: 6 px a side and no gap
between them (they had 10 px and 2 px), and the count 5 px from its word
(it had 8 px). Measured in the same Chromium at 320 px, they need 275 px
with one digit (276 on Approvals) and 282 with two (283), so up to 99
waiting fit on every page. A three-digit count still runs past, and the
row still scrolls. From 375 px the links keep their room, which holds two
digits with 19 px to spare. Each link stays at least 50 × 32 px. No word,
count or script changed; this is presentation only.

Tests: `css-nav-fits.test.ts` covers the model (`nav-row.ts`) of the row
from the stylesheet's own numbers, with the words' widths as that Chromium

- Chromium's numbers before (at 375 px, the old room) and after (320 px);
- every window from 320 to 640 px, every page current, with nothing and

- the row still scrolls;
- from 375 px the links keep their room;
- the page in jsdom draws what the model reads.

Four of the five fail on the old page. Stack
`tests/stack/nav-fits-count.test.ts` (`secrets`) runs a real arbiter whose

*History joins the links (2026-10-18).* History became a fifth page link
(§4.25ae *History is a page link*), and five links do not fit a phone's

with one waiting at 375 px, in a 343 px row. So at 640 px and narrower the **Home** word is
hidden (`display: none`): the brand *Mandu* beside it already links Home,

digit and 282/283 with two, so up to 99 waiting still fit on every page
with 5 px to spare. Every link stays at least 50 × 32 px.

Wider than 640 px the links share the bar with the brand (66 px) and the

waiting, and at 641 px they left "Protection on" 42 px of its 94: the
words ran past the status's box. From 641 to 767 px the links have 7 px a

needed before (368), so no status has less room than it had. From 768 px

Tests: `css-nav-fits.test.ts` adds the hidden Home word, the 50 px floor,
and the bar from 641 to 1280 px (`nav-row.ts` `bar`, with the brand's and
each status's measured widths): every page current, nothing to 99

**The tiles fill their rows evenly (2026-10-15; app.css).** A session's
page opens with one tile per count (`#agent-facts`, home.js
`renderAgent`). In the `secrets` mode it draws 1 to 6: reached the AI
unmasked, masked, read before marked, blocked, sent and waiting. `.tiles`
is `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(180px, 100%), 1fr))` with 12 px gaps. That
puts as many tiles in a row as fit and leaves the rest for the next row, so
one tile could sit alone under the others. A headless Chromium over the
served page (the first-session tour's session, its tiles cloned to 1–7,
at 16 widths) measured these breakpoints. The tiles span `#main`'s column,
`min(100%, 1040px)` less `clamp(16px, 4vw, 48px)` a side, so two fit from
a 405 px window, three from 614, four from 822, and five from 1031 to
1150 px (the column is 948–957 px there). The tour's four tiles drew as
3 + 1 at 614–821 px. At 720 px, half a 1440 px screen, "send with a real
value filled in" sat alone under three, beside two empty cells. Five
tiles drew as 4 + 1 from 822 px, a 1280 px desktop included. Six drew as
4 + 2 there, and as 5 + 1 at 1031–1150 px.

Now the rows stay as few as auto-fit's, and are filled evenly. Three
width queries count the tiles with
`.tiles:has(> .tile:nth-child(N):last-child)`:

- four tiles at 614–821 px: `repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr))`, which draws
  2 + 2 with each tile 276–372 px wide. At 720 px each label fits on one
  line, and the block is 39 px shorter;
- five or six tiles from 822 px: `repeat(3, …)`, which draws 3 + 2 and
  3 + 3. Each tile is 244 px or wider, wider than before;
- five tiles at 1031–1150 px: `repeat(5, …)`. Five fit in one row there,
  so they keep it.

Everything else is unchanged: 1–3 tiles at every width; four below 614 px
and from 822 px; five and six below 822 px; one tile a row below 405 px. No
tile is narrower than 180 px, and no column is empty. A browser without
`:has()` drops the three rules and draws auto-fit. After the change, the
same Chromium probe draws every arrangement as above. Presentation only: no
route, word, focus rule or server text changed.

*On a phone (2026-10-18; app.css).* Below a 405 px window, #main's
column (the window less 16 px a side, 358 px at 390 px) fits no two 180 px
tiles, so auto-fit gave each tile a whole row. Measured in a headless
Chromium, the tour's four tiles took 381 px at 390 px and 401 px at 320 px
(the long label wraps there), nearly half an 844 px phone screen, and *Your
secrets* started below the first screen. Now `@media (max-width: 404px)`
lowers the tiles' minimum to `minmax(min(130px, 100%), 1fr)`, still
auto-fit. Under 614 px, then, two to six tiles sit two to a row at every
window from 304 px: 2 + 2 for four, 2 + 1 for three, 2 + 2 + 2 for six. A
tile is 130–180 px wide below 405 px, 138 px at 320 px and 173 px at
390 px. From 405 px the 180 px tiles already sat two to a row, so nothing
changes there. The four tiles' block is now 224 px tall at 390 px and
243 px at 320 px. That is the 224 px it already was at 405–412 px. A long
label ("secret the AI read before it was marked a secret") wraps inside
its tile over three or four lines, and the tiles of a row keep one height.
The same probe (1 to 6 tiles at 11 widths from 280 to 613 px) cut no
label word and widened no page past its window.

Two choices. First, the rule lowers auto-fit's minimum and does not set
`repeat(2, …)`. One tile then still takes the row (auto-fit collapses the
empty column), no `:has()` is needed, and a window under 304 px, where two
tiles would cut their words, falls back to one to a row. Three never fit
below 405 px. Second, the odd count's last tile keeps its own column and
does not span the row. That is how three and five tiles already drew at
405–613 px, so a phone draws them the same way. Presentation only.

Tests: `css-tiles-rows.test.ts`, with the model `tiles-rows.ts`. jsdom has
no layout, so the model computes the rows from the stylesheet's own
numbers, over files-name-room.ts `pageColumn`, which is `#main`'s column
factored out of its rows' model. Unknown `.tiles` rules or columns throw.

- E1: for 1–6 tiles at every window from 320 to 1600 px, the rows are as
  few as auto-fit's, and no row holds two tiles more than another.
- E2: no tile that shares its row is under 180 px, and no column is empty.
- E3: wherever auto-fit's rows were already even, the stylesheet draws
  auto-fit's columns. Exactly the windows above change.
- E4: the session page in jsdom draws its 3–6 tiles, and nothing else, in
  the columns each width's styles give them.

E1, E3 and E4 fail on the old page; E2 is a guard. Stack
`tests/stack/agent-tiles-rows.test.ts` (secrets) runs a real arbiter and
the real anthropic-proxy on its production client. One session reads
`deploy/staging.conf` before the Rules page marks it, and a `.env` whose
key the proxy masks. The real egress gate then refuses the key's send to an
unbound host and asks for an OK. A real dashboard over the production
adapter serves the session's page, whose four tiles (masked, read before
marked, blocked, waiting) compute two columns as a 720 px window applies
the served styles, and auto-fit at 613 and 822 px. The served stylesheet
passes E1. The model never got the value, and no page or answer holds it,
the staging file's bytes or a token.

Not covered:

- seven tiles. They happen only in the frozen masking modes, which add the
  untrusted items' tile. They still draw 3 + 3 + 1 at 614–821 px and 5 + 2
  at 1031–1150 px;
- three tiles at 405–613 px stay 2 + 1. Three in a row would be under
  180 px;
- a phone below 405 px keeps one tile a row: the tour's four take 381 px
  of an 844 px screen. Two columns would be 138–173 px wide, under the
  180 px minimum, so that is a design call.

**An empty list never says nothing waits over a rule change
(2026-10-12).** The nav badge and Home's *Approvals waiting (N)* count the
questions and the rule changes your agent asked for (`renderTopStatus`:
the waiting asks plus `S.proposals`). The questions list's empty line knew
only the questions. A headless Chromium at 1280 and 390 px, with the
agent's binding of `.env` to a host waiting and no question, drew Home as
"Approvals waiting (1)", then "Nothing is waiting for you.", then "1 rule
change your agent asked for is in Approvals": two lines apart, the page
said 1 and nothing. Approvals drew the request's live *Allow* / *Not now*
under *Rule changes your agent asked for*, and right under it *Waiting for
your answer*: "Nothing is waiting for you.".

Now, while a rule change waits and no question does, the line on Home and
on Approvals reads **"No question is waiting for you."** The page calls a
waiting ask a question everywhere else ("One question is waiting for
you.", "2 more questions in Approvals"), so the line says what is true of
its list. With nothing waiting at all it still reads "Nothing is waiting
for you.". `renderAsks` takes a fourth argument, `changesWait`, which
`renderHomeWaiting` and `renderApprovals` pass as `S.proposals.length >
0`. Home's draw key already held the requests' count. Approvals' key
(`sameAsDrawn('approvals', …)`) now holds whether a rule change waits while
no question does, so a request a poll brings, or one answered in another
tab, draws the line again. A rule change that comes while a question waits
draws nothing again: no line shows then. The line is keyed
(`data-empty="questions"`, `placeKey`), so a focus on it (the landing of
the last answer, *An answer keeps the focus in its list*) stays on it when
a poll draws it with the other words. Before, the redrawn line would have
been matched by its words and lost the focus. The agent page's *Needs your
OK* lists one agent's questions; since the same day it links the rule
changes that agent asked for and says "No question is waiting for you."
over them, and another agent's request leaves it as it was (*A rule change
and the agent that asked*, below). Presentation only: no route,
count, answer or server text changed. The inspector's Approvals says the
same, with a link to this page (§4.34 *A rule change your agent asked for
is never "nothing"*).

- nothing waiting at all, and a question beside a rule change (no line),

- Approvals under the request's card, then *Not now* turns the line back;
- a poll that brings a request, or takes it away;
- a request that comes while a question waits leaves the cards as drawn;
- the focus after the last answer on Home lands on the new words;
- a focus on the line stays on it when its words change;
- the agent page unchanged.

**A rule change and the agent that asked (2026-10-12).** A headless
Chromium at 1280 and 390 px, with three agents running and the first one's
request to let `.env` be sent to a host waiting, drew the nav badge
"Approvals 1" and Home's "1 rule change your agent asked for is in

card on Approvals, where you decide whether to loosen a rule, was the one

what the agent was doing", and the Rules page's origin line links the
session of a change the agent made (`ruleOrigins`' `session`, §4.25i). The
cause was the projection: the arbiter records the request's `sessionKey`,
and `toProposalCard` dropped it.

Now `ProposalCardVM.session` is the session of the agent that asked: the
request's `sessionKey` when `requestedBy` is an agent (`agent:…`), and null
for you, the setup assistant, a held change to policy.yaml (§4.6) and a
request with no session recorded. The listing is read signed out too, as
the origins listing is, and a session id is no secret (Home's agent links
carry it). The product page uses it twice:

- **The agent page** (`drawAgentPage`) counts the waiting requests whose
  `session` is its own (`agentChanges`; never a held disk change). With one,
  *Needs your OK* shows: its questions, or "No question is waiting for
  you." (the words of Home and Approvals, *An empty list never says nothing
  waits over a rule change*), then the link **"1 rule change this agent

  answer: *Allow* and *Not now* stay on Approvals, the one place that shows
  what the change would let. The tiles still count the questions. The
  page's draw key (`sameAsDrawn('agent', …)`) holds that count, so a
  request a poll brings, or one answered in another tab, draws the page
  again; a focus on the link stays on it while it reads the same, and goes
  to the section's heading when its count changes (*The poll keeps the
  focus*: never another action). Another agent's page is unchanged.
- **The request's card** (`proposalCard`) says **"See what the agent was
  doing"** in its footer, in a question card's place (left, the answers
  right), and opens the agent page of that session at its top
  (`askLink(session, null)`, as the origin line does). A request with no
  session has no link. A wide change's card keeps its "Type ALLOW" field
  after the link. The link, the answers and that field are named by the
  request (*The answers on a request card name their request*).

An agent could name another session's key when it asks; the link would then
open that session's page, which shows only that session's own record, as
the origin line would. The id is drawn as text and compared as a value,
never spliced into markup or a selector. Presentation only: no route, verb,
count or arbiter answer changed; the card carries one more field.

**A rule change you asked for is never credited to your agent
(2026-10-15).** The product page's own writes (a rule's menu, Save under

propose on the admin channel and approve at once (`applyAsHuman`). When
the approval fails, the request stays waiting: policy.yaml changed on disk
just before (the arbiter refuses the write as stale, "(the proposal is
still pending)"), or the dashboard stopped between the two calls. Run
2026-10-15-0601 reproduced the first on the real routes: a hand edit, then
a rule's menu. Approvals then drew the request as **"You wants to change a
rule"**. The page's own note ("Changed on the Rules page (remove)") sat
under **"Your agent says"**, below the heading **"Rule changes your agent
asked for"**, and Home linked it as **"1 rule change your agent asked for
is in Approvals"**. So the person read that the agent had asked to loosen
a rule, when they had asked for it themselves. The heading said the same
over a held change to policy.yaml (§4.6), which Home already words as
waiting for you.

Now `ProposalCardVM.byAgent` is true only when `requestedBy` is `agent:…`
and the change is not held on disk. The arbiter sets `agent:<session>` on
every request over the data socket, and on no other
(`policy-agent-ops.ts proposeOne`), so no agent can be shown as you. For

- the block's heading reads **"Rule changes waiting for you"** while any

- Home's line reads **"1 rule change waits for you in Approvals"** ("2 rule
  changes wait …") in the same case, as it already did for a held change;
- an Allow answered `refiled` says "The rules changed since this was asked;

A card without `byAgent` reads as the agent's, as every card did before.
An agent's request reads exactly as before. Presentation only: no route,
verb, count or arbiter answer changed; the card carries one more field.
Whether the page should withdraw its own request when the approval fails
is a separate question for the maintainer, and this wording holds either

**A wide change says what is open (2026-10-19).** A wide rule change asks
you to type ALLOW before **Allow** works. Until now the only reason its
card gave was "This change has no limit on one side.", the code's own

390 px, with the agent asking the real `policyPropose` for `allow-connect
host: *`, drew the row "Let your agent's programs connect to any address"
and, at the foot beside the field, that phrase: it named neither the open
side nor why the word was asked. Describe's suggestion card said "One of
these changes has no limit on one side." without saying which one.

Now `overBroadWhy(edits)` (`view-model/policy-proposals.ts`, pure, beside
`isOverBroad`) gives one sentence per wide edit, in edit order, from the
row grammar's own words (`connectTarget`, the release row's "masked data
from … to …"):

- a connect to `*`: "This lets your agent's programs connect to any
  address." (with a port, "any address on port 443");
- a connect to `*.example.org`: "… connect to any address that matches
  `*.example.org`.";
- an allowed send with no source or `from: *`: "This lets masked data from
  anywhere be sent to `api.example.com`."; with `to: *`: "… from
  `docs.python.org` be sent anywhere." (both open: one sentence);
- a wildcard trusted origin, on the frozen integrity axis, keeps the old
  words; a far "your own" model gives no sentence, since its warning says
  it.

At most two sentences, then "And N more wide changes." `toProposalCard`
sends them as `overBroadWhy`; the Approvals foot (`home.js wideWhy`) draws
them, each name whole (`fitWords`), then "Type ALLOW if you mean it." A
card with a warning keeps "Read the warning above before you allow this.",
after any sentence another wide edit of it gives; a card with no sentences
(an older server) keeps the old words. On Describe each row carries its
own `overBroadWhy` and the suggestion the foot's; a wide row gets the
marker **"Wide: type ALLOW"** beside its words, and the foot says what the
wide rows open, the same way.

#### 4.25b "What happened": the product page borrows the paired rows

**What it is.** `buildStory` (pure, `view-model/agent-page.ts`) tells one
session from `vm.paired` (§4.2f) and the dual-lanes steps its rows reference,
so the product page shows blocks, every turn and the sandboxed reader's
exchange, which a flat one-line-per-call story missed.

- **One card per turn**: *You asked* (or "Before your first question" for
  workspace setup), a one-line plain summary ("Mandu blocked 1 action and
  masked 1 item. The sandboxed reader answered 1 question for the AI."),
  toned by the worst outcome (red for blocked or unmasked, amber for
  waiting), the steps, the reply, and a muted "In the background: …" line
  (§4.2f's Background fold; see *The background line* below).
- **Steps.** A tool row keeps its family sentence (the sandboxed reader quotes
  its instruction); an OS `action` row (blocks, denials, violations,
  uncorrelated file actions) gets `osSentence` ("Mandu blocked a connection to
  `example.com`"); interim AI messages are muted "The agent said" lines; the
  seed is "Prepared the workspace: N files were masked". No repeat counts.
  The kernel guard's FILE decisions are worded as files (2026-10-11): its
  binary hosts the file guard beside the connect guard and records both as
  `net_action` (net-supervisor `events.rs`), so its git-lock refusal read
  "Mandu blocked a connection to the network". The first-session tour on
  OpenCode met it: after `mandu policy suggest` labelled a file, the next
  launch's page opened with it, for OpenCode's own snapshot repository
  (`~/.local/share/opencode/snapshot/…`), which held the file from the
  earlier session. `dual-lanes.ts` `fileGuardOf` reads the producers' exact
  reasons into `DualOsStep.fileGuard`, and `osSentence` says "Mandu kept
  git from reading a history that may hold a secret you marked, in
  `…/<last four segments>`" (note: git does not work there for the rest of
  the session; the next launch prepares a copy without the secret, true of a
  work tree, which the refusal registers). OpenCode's snapshot store is
  said apart (`…/share/opencode/snapshot/…`, 2026-10-11): it is a git
  directory, never registered or prepared, so that note was wrong for it
  (the notice came back every session, confidentiality.md §7.2a, K15):
  "Mandu kept OpenCode from reading its own snapshot history (its undo),
  which holds a file you marked secret, in `…/<last four segments>`" (note:
  nothing needs doing; OpenCode's undo of changes from before the label
  stops working, once OpenCode has packed that history its undo of new
  changes too (K15b), and this comes back in each session where OpenCode reads
  that history; to stop it, remove that folder outside Mandu), "Mandu
  blocked deleting or renaming a protected file: `name`" (`protect:`),
  "Mandu blocked a change to a protected file: `name`" (write-protect), and
  "A program got the placeholder copy of `name`, not the real file" (a
  network or FUSE mount could see the read). No host-shaped *Why*.
  A refused Unix socket is worded the same way (2026-10-11): the walk with
  Claude Code started inside tmux met it when the agent ran `tmux` and the
  guard's allow-list refused `unix:/tmp/tmux-1007/default` (the tmux server
  runs outside the session and starts commands on request, so the refusal
  is intended: usage.md, guarantees.md); the page said "Mandu blocked 2
  actions … Mandu blocked a connection to the network". `fileGuardOf` reads
  `guard_unix_refusal_event`'s text (`connect to unix:<socket>[ by <exe>] —
  REFUSED (unix-socket allow-list: …)`) as `local-socket`, with the socket
  (a path, an `@name`, or none for the command box's datagram) and the
  program's base name, and `osSentence` says "Mandu kept the AI's command
  `tmux` from reaching a local program's socket: `/tmp/tmux-1007/default`"
  (icon *run*, *Blocked*; note: a program that runs outside Mandu listens
  there, so a command sent through it would run outside Mandu's
  protection). Only the allow-list's text is read so: the guard's other
  `unix:` refusals (a process holding a secret, a secret socket's readers,
  WSL interop) still read as a connection, with their own rule's *Why*.
- **Mandu's own tools** (2026-10-05). When the agent called Mandu's rule
  tools (the mandu-policy server's read, test and propose,
  policy-surface.md §8.5.1), the step read "Used `mandu-policy
  mandu_policy_propose`". Yet the record holds what was asked and what
  Mandu answered. `mandu-tool-words.ts` now says both.
  - **What was asked.** A propose call reads "Asked Mandu to make
    `/home/u/proj/.env` a secret hidden from the AI". Each edit is in the
    Approvals card's grammar (`editRow`). Several edits read "Asked Mandu
    for 2 rule changes: make …; trust …", with three spelled out and the
    rest counted. A prompt exception's pattern is hidden, as on the card.
    The agent's `reason` is never shown, since it is untrusted text. A read
    call reads "Read your Mandu rules". A test call reads "Asked Mandu
    whether data from `X` could be sent to `Y`".
  - **What Mandu answered.** The note under the step:

    - "Nothing changed: your rules already said this."
    - "Not applied: it would loosen protection, so Mandu asked for your OK

    - "Mandu did not apply it, so nothing changed." (invalid, stale, or too
      many waiting).
    - A test call: "Only a question: nothing was sent or changed. Mandu

      "that it would be blocked").

    - Only the spellings the arbiter's trust gate vouches for count

      the same name keeps "Used …".
    - The answer is read only from the server's fixed-shape answer for that
      same tool. A masked, missing or malformed answer gives no note.
    - The step stays `plain`, with a shield icon, so no count, tone or fold
      changes.
    - Values are code, each masked item a chip, cut at 120 characters.
      Paths are shown as the agent wrote them, as on the Approvals card.

    - the file gate's: a key file, a file outside the agent's folders, a

- **A call Mandu rewrote reads as what it stopped** (2026-10-07, nightly
  run 1430). The model proxies enforce an exec or net block by rewriting
  the call before the agent gets it, and their sniffers record the call as
  rewritten. The exec gate turns a command into `echo '<notice>' 1>&2;
  exit 77` (`blockSentinelCommand`, both proxies; an argv field becomes
  `["/bin/sh", "-c", …]`). The net gate turns a fetch's URL into one on the
  reserved host `blocked.mandu.invalid` and a search's query into its
  notice. The step worded that input, so in a session that had read a
  secret (where every command is gated) the page said "Ran `echo
  'mandu-exec-gate: blocked, nothing ran: this session has read a secret,
  an…`" over "Mandu stopped it.", "Opened a web page on
  `blocked.mandu.invalid`" with a why about "this place", and "Searched the
  web for `mandu-net-gate: …`". Now (`view-model/gate-rewrite.ts`,
  `agent-page.ts` `rewrittenCall`):
  - "Mandu stopped a command before it ran". **Why:** the rule's words when
    the page words its rule, else the reason the notice gives (the
    proxies' `plainBlockWords`): "This session read a secret, and Mandu
    cannot be sure this command stays off the network. Start a new session
    for work that needs it."; "You said no to running it earlier."; the
    service not answering; "Running it needs your OK.". The integrity
    axis's reason and the catch-all give none. The arbiter records the
    session-gate block under the allowing rule's id
    (`exec:no-symbol-in-command`), so the notice is what says why there.
  - "Mandu blocked opening a web page on `evil.example`", "The request was
    never sent.", and a why that names the host. The host is the one the
    call's net check recorded, kept as `DualGate.target` (§4.2f): the
    model proxy's `WebFetch → <host>`, the net-proxy's `destination`. A
    check that named none, or a host holding a token, reads "Mandu blocked
    opening a web page".
  - "Mandu blocked a web search", "The AI's search words were never
    sent.".
  - **Only what the record backs.** A command is the sentinel only when it
    is nothing else: the whole command, its notice one single-quoted
    string (the proxies strip every quote from it), so no other program
    can hide in a step the page calls stopped. The words need a check of
    the rewrite's own kind (an exec check for a command, a net check for a
    fetch or search) that stopped the call. A model can write the sentinel
    itself, and Codex's checks are recorded with `callId: ""` and never
    join their call; both keep the old words. The proxies record only the
    rewrite (`makeExecGate` keeps `Bash.command`, not the command), so
    the page cannot show the command the AI wrote.
  - The inspector keeps the call as it ran: the rewrite is its trace.

  Tests: `gate-rewrite.test.ts` (the forms and their near misses),

  `tests/stack/dashboard-blocked-call-words.test.ts` (the real
  anthropic-proxy blocks a command, a fetch and a search in a session that
  read a secret; parity with both proxies' real sentinels; the oracle).

  *Your secrets* called an OpenCode or OpenClaw `read` of a secret file,

  that held a secret", where Claude Code's `Read` reads "The file `~/…`".
  Now one table (`view-model/tool-family.ts`) names every supported

  - **The step:** "Read `partner-token.md`", "Opened a web page on
    `docs.example.com`", "Searched the web for `acme payments`", "Ran `git
    status`", "Listed the files in `src`" (the folder the agent runs in,
    `.`, reads "Listed files"). Monitor's socket form runs nothing and
    keeps "Used `Monitor`". A tool no family covers keeps "Used <tool>",
    the agent's own word (Mandu's own rule tools and its in-context read
    have their own words, *Mandu's own tools* and *A request for a
    secret's real value* above).
  - ***Your secrets*:** every file-read tool (`Read`, `read`, `read_file`)
    names its file. A search or a listing names a folder, so it never reads
    "The file …".
  - **Approvals and Rules** (`rule-words.ts` `dataWords`): data from any
    agent's shell reads "the output of “…”".
  - **The inspector:** a card's right half is headed by the file for every
    agent's read ("`.env` contains", §4.2f), not only for Claude Code's
    `Read`. Its step rail and card controls name every family's calls
    from its own copy of this table, which a test keeps in step (§4.33 *A
    step names what it touched*, 2026-10-13).
  - **A patch names its files** (2026-10-09). `apply_patch` (Codex's
    freeform and JSON forms, OpenClaw's, OpenCode's) names its files only in
    its patch text, so it read "Edited `a file`", and the openai-proxy
    recorded nothing for Codex's freeform form. Now the proxy records it as
    `apply_patch({"input": <patch>})`, its JSON form's shape, as the model
    wrote it (supported-agents.md §6.2, "A freeform patch is one call"), and
    `view-model/patch-files.ts` reads the files off the patch's headers
    (`*** Update File:`, `*** Add File:`, `*** Delete File:`, an Update's
    `*** Move to:`), from `{input}`, OpenCode's `{patchText}`, the request
    transcript's bare string or the text itself. A header is a line that
    starts with its marker, so a file whose content holds a header's text
    is never read as one; the reader names files and decides nothing.
    - **The step:** "Edited `config.ts`, created `setup.md`, deleted
      `legacy.ts`", "Moved `a.ts` to `b.ts`": each file by its base name,
      grouped by what the patch does to it (edited, created, moved,
      deleted), the first three named and the rest counted ("and 2 more
      files"). A masked item in a path is a chip. A patch that names no file
      keeps "Edited `a file`".
    - **The inspector:** the step carries `patchFiles` (`dual-lanes`), and
      its card a line under the args: "Files in the patch: `src/app.ts`
      changed · `docs/setup.md` added · `src/a.ts` moved to `src/b.ts`",
      each path as the AI wrote it.
    - **Signed out** nothing changes: the files come from the call's
      arguments as the AI wrote them, which the projection already serves.
  - **A patch in a code cell** (2026-10-17). A Codex code-mode `exec` cell
    that calls `tools.apply_patch(…)` was recorded by its
    `tools.exec_command` literals only, so its patch named no file, and a
    cell that only patched read "Ran `a command`" (the step took the cell's
    tool, `exec`, off the next request's transcript). Now the openai-proxy
    reads the cell's source (`cell-patch-calls.ts`; supported-agents.md
    §6.2, "A patch in a code cell is a call too") and records each patch
    whose text is certain as `apply_patch({"input": <patch>})`, the record
    above, under the cell's call id, after the cell's exec literals. Certain
    means written out in the cell: a string or hole-free template literal,
    a one-field `{input: …}` object, or a name bound once by a top-level
    `const` and used nowhere else (`const patch = "…"; await
    tools.apply_patch(patch)`, the form a live model writes). The reader
    lexes the cell (strings, templates, comments, regular expressions), so a
    call written inside a string or a comment is none, and it reads
    nothing from a cell whose `/` only more than one token could place.
    - **The step** stays the cell's one step (one call id, one result).
      `tool-calls.ts` `extractToolUses`: the last record names it, but a
      patch never renames a call another tool named, since the cell ran
      that tool and its gates speak of it; every patch's args are kept
      (`patches`), and `dual-lanes` gives the step the files of all of them
      (`patchFilesOf`, each once). A cell that ran a command and patched
      reads "Ran `npm test` and edited `config.ts`, created `setup.md`"; a
      cell of patches only, "Moved `a.ts` to `b.ts`, deleted `legacy.ts`".
      The inspector's card lists the files under the args, as for any patch
      step.
    - **Symbols and signing out:** as above. The path is the AI's own text,
      a placeholder a chip on the page and kept as written in the trace;
      nothing is resolved. The patch text was already in the record: the
      next request's transcript carries the cell's source.
    - **Not covered:** a patch whose text the cell computes (a
      concatenation, a template with a `${…}` hole, a function's result, a
      `let`, a name used twice), a patch run through an alias of `tools` or
      a computed member (`tools[name]`), a cell the reader gives up on, and
      sessions recorded before 2026-10-17 (their records hold no cell patch;
      the step keeps the exec's words).

- **A command shows its masked items** (2026-10-05). The agent's paste
  command used to read ``Ran `curl … -H "X-Key: [masked]…` `` right above
  "Sent a request to `paste.example` with your secret `PASTE_KEY` filled
  in", so a reader could not tell that the AI wrote the masked `PASTE_KEY`,
  not the key. Worse, `shorten` cut the raw command at 80 characters before
  `maskTokens` ran. When the cut fell inside a token's hash, the page showed
  `$MDU:nomodel_Read[3…`, against its own no-token rule. `codeParts` now
  builds a command, path or query (and an OS step's exec or file subject)
  as code, with each masked item a chip in it. The cut counts a chip at the
  width it draws, and a chip is drawn whole or not at all.
  - A secret's chip carries its name (`StoryPart.name`, the send steps'
    `secretShortName` label): `X-Key: ⟨PASTE_KEY⟩`, titled "Your secret
    PASTE_KEY, masked: the AI never got the real value". A secret with no
    name keeps the `secret` chip, and anything else keeps `masked`. Without
    the session's scope, a twin prefix still reads as a secret. A secret
    the AI read before it was marked never claims "never" (*A secret the
    AI read before it was marked*, below).
  - The step's note says "The AI used the masked version of your secret,
    not its real value." ("the masked versions of your secrets" when it
    holds more than one; one secret used twice counts once), in §4.25u's
    words ("masked", never "placeholder"). The recorded input holds the
    token. A block, a wait or a leak keeps its own note.
  - home.js `sentenceNode` draws a chip next to a code part inside that
    `<code>`, so the command reads as one piece. Two code parts with no
    chip between them stay two.
  - A shell variable such as `$GITHUB_TOKEN` stays as written. The page
    cannot know what it held, so it claims nothing about it.

  split whenever its text held a placeholder. But the page never fills in a

  replies drew the same text twice. The right half was headed "You saw,
  with the masked items filled in", over the same `secret` chip, and read
  as a contradiction. `agent-page.ts` `storyReply` now splits a reply only
  when what you saw differs from what the AI wrote, as `StoryReply.ai`'s
  type already said.
  - **One card.** A reply whose masked items are all secrets is one "The
    agent replied" card.
  - **A line names the secrets.** Under the reply (`StoryReply.kept`), in

    "a secret of yours". A split reply that also held a secret has the line
    under its right half. A secret the AI read before it was marked adds

    recorded) leaves the reply one card too (`StoryReply.unresolved`). It
    gets the step's hidden-box line: signed out the sign-in note, signed in

  token, and the page does not resolve a secret. It says nothing of what
  the person's terminal showed, which only the session's reply-filter
  events record (*Your secrets* says it per secret). Names only, never a

  Trace still draws both halves of such a reply. Tests:
  `agent-page.test.ts`, `home-js-agent.test.ts`,
  `session-page-record.test.ts` (the served tour).

- **A command's output is never named by a piece of the command**
  (2026-10-07, nightly run 1030; the work ledger's tour item 7). The
  proxies record a masked result's origin as its call's locator
  (`originFor`): a file path for a file tool, but the COMMAND for a shell
  tool, and an address or query for a web tool. `secretShortName` took the

  `set -a && . ./.env && … /v1/customers -u "$STRIPE_KEY:"`, masked whole
  because it names `./.env` (confidentiality.md §7.1, the path-derived

  - an environment variable (`env:`);
  - the base name of an origin that is a file.

  named the same item "Output of a `Bash` step that held a secret", and
  its right half read "The result held a secret of yours.", until both
  said why (the next two bullets). A `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa`
  that read "your secret `id_rsa`" by luck now reads the same way; the
  command above it still shows the path. The count was already right. The
  page reads no `secretTaint` (the path-derived one says `level: "public"`):
  the symbol's own `no-model` level counts it as 1 masked secret on the
  page's tile, on Home and in the inspector. The AI half of such a step also
  reads whole, "Got [secret] in place of the result.". The proxy's
  `[mandu:secret]` note that follows the placeholder is Mandu's, not part
  of the result (`maskedResultParts` drops the step's recorded note from the
  end), so it no longer reads "Got the result with [secret] in place of the

  the real arbiter, both proxies and the dashboard signed out:
  `tests/stack/dashboard-command-output-name.test.ts`.

  - **A program of it read a secret file** (plan 10 rule (i), or a value

  - Files read `~/…` under the dashboard's home (`buildStory`'s `home`,

  - Only when no item the result held has a name (a twin's field still

    (fail-closed, session, a refusal, a twin, a listed reader's release, a

  - Unchanged: the AI half, the reveal box, the mark, the counts, and the

- **A refusal is not a mask** (2026-10-05). The tour's blocked curl (10:38)
  read "Got the result with [secret] in place of the real value. *Secret
  hidden*. The result held your secret `STRIPE_KEY`.", and its turn read
  "… and hid your secret `STRIPE_KEY` from the AI." But its result was
  Mandu's fail-closed refusal. That refusal names the placeholder the AI
  had put in the command, both in what the tool returned and in what the
  AI got. Its only `[mandu:secret]` line was `refused:` ("curl tried to
  connect out and Mandu refused the connection, nothing was sent"). Nothing
  in it was kept from the AI. Two rules now apply.
  - **A refusal note is not a mask.** `noteMasks`: a secret note counts as
    "a secret was masked" unless every line of it is a refusal: `refused:`,
    `denied:` or `held:` (rewrite-request.ts `buildSecretNote`; the last
    two since 2026-10-07, below). Any other or unknown form keeps the
    masked reading.
  - **An echoed placeholder is not hidden.** `heldTokens`: a token in what
    the AI got counts as kept from it, unless the call's own input sent it
    and the tool's own result (`resultHuman`) holds it as written. Mandu's
    refusal and a command printing its argument are such echoes.
    - A token the tool's own result lacks still counts. An example is a
      reply that carried the real value, which the proxy masked back to the
      same token.
    - So does one the call never sent, such as a twin's placeholder.
    - No input or no original recorded: every token counts, as before.
    - A masked result's AI half counts only these as real values ("… in
      place of the real value", not "2 real values" with an echo beside).

  So the step is `plain`, with the masked-use note ("The AI used the masked
  version of your secret, not its real value.") and no halves. Its turn
  reads "Mandu blocked 1 request that carried your secret `STRIPE_KEY`."
  What a click may reveal is withheld as before: any secret note or any
  secret token in what the AI got, an echoed one included. No count
  changes: the tiles count Your secrets and the steps blocked or sent, and
  this step was neither. Tests:
  `agent-page.test.ts`, `session-page-record.test.ts` (unit and component,
  the tour's 10:38 turn). `heldTokens` lives in `view-model/held-tokens.ts`
  (2026-10-05), so the inspector's paired rows decide the same step with
  the same rule (§4.2f "A placeholder echoed is not a mask").
- **A refused read is a block, not a mask** (2026-10-07). When the guard
  refuses a program's open of a secret file, the arbiter records the
  refusal in its log only, so no gate event joins the step. The proxy
  forwards the program's own failure text ("`cat: …/.env: Permission
  denied`": every secret open in the tree refused, no registered value in
  it, plan 10 §11.8's `deniedOnly` release) with a note line: `denied:`
  (the program may not read the file) or `held:`
  (the open waited for the person's OK on Approvals until its ceiling
  passed; the row stays open). Such a step read "*Secret hidden*. A secret
  was masked before the AI saw it.", its turn "Mandu hid 1 secret from the
  AI.", and no tile counted it. Nothing was masked: Mandu stopped a program
  from reading the file.
  - `refusedReadNote`: a note with no masking line and at least one
    `denied:` or `held:` line makes the step `blocked`, after the checks
    that come first (a gate's block, a wait, read as it was, the sandboxed
    reader). Its note says what Mandu did, counted, never a program or a
    path: "Mandu stopped a program from reading a secret file, so the AI got
    the command's output without it."; "Mandu held a program's read of a
    secret file and asked for your OK. Nobody answered in time, so the AI
    got the command's output without it."; several read "Mandu stopped 2
    reads of secret files, … One of them waited for your OK, and nobody
    answered in time."
  - So the page's "actions blocked" tile and Home's row count it
    (`storyCounts`; the tile's own words: "a command, a file or a send"),
    and the turn's line says what it was: "Mandu stopped 1 read of a
    secret file." (reads counted as the notes count them, `denied` +
    `held`, so one command refused two files is 2 reads; *The summary
    names the secrets* below has the rule beside other blocks).
  - A note that also masks (`masked:` from a tree that did read the
    secret, a twin, an unknown form) keeps "Secret hidden": that claim is
    true, and the step does not also say a read was refused.
  - The `note:` form (a listed reader's output released by its rule) still
    reads as masked, as any form this rule does not read; wording that
    release is open.
  - **The inspector counts them too** (2026-10-07, nightly run 0830). Its
    counts read only gates and verdicts, so over the same session it said
    "1 step blocked" where the page said 3, and drew both commands as
    plain `Bash` calls. The note rule now lives in
    `view-model/secret-note.ts` (`noteMasks`, `readRefusals`,
    `refusedReadWords`), shared by the page and the inspector's
    projection: such a tool step carries `readRefused` (`{denied, held}`,
    counts only; read off the result the AI got at its own turn, never a
    later re-send), and its paired row `refusedRead`, the page's sentence.
    `stepBlocked` (session-counts.ts and its mirror in `dev/js/app.js`)
    counts the step blocked, and `stepFiledAsk` counts a held read as an
    ask too, since the arbiter filed an Approvals row for it. So the
    session list's chips and the header (§4.33), the step rail's marks
    (`blocked`; a held read `asked` + `blocked`), the path's *Mandu
    checked* stop and the 🛡 card's "other actions blocked" (§4.16) all
    count them, and the tool card has a blocked check line with the
    page's words and a `secret note` pill, since no guard event recorded
    it (§4.2f).
  Tests: `agent-page.test.ts` and `secret-note.test.ts` (unit: the rule,
  the words, the projection), `session-counts.test.ts` (the counts and
  the client/server step rules), `app-js-dual-lanes.test.ts` (the
  inspector's header, path, rail, card and 🛡 card),
  `session-walkthrough.test.ts` (component: the served page and the
  served inspector over `readRefusals`), and
  `tests/stack/dashboard-refused-read.test.ts` (a real arbiter in

  and, in the same turn, a `curl` of a registered key the real net-proxy
  refuses; the real dashboard signed out: both reads blocked on the agent
  page, the turn's line "Mandu blocked 1 request that carried your secret
  `STRIPE_KEY` and stopped 2 reads of secret files.", Home counts 3,
  `/api/events` and the sidebar's row count 3 blocked and 2 asks, and
  neither value reaches the model, api.stripe.com or any route).
- **The summary names the secrets** (2026-10-05). The turn's one line used
  to count steps ("Mandu blocked 1 action and hid 1 secret. 2 requests left
  this machine with a real value filled in, …") right under *Your secrets*,
  which names two. A reader could not tell which secret was hidden, whose
  value went out, or what the block stopped. `turnSummary` now takes the
  items each step names (`StepItems`: what a masked result held, what a send
  carried or was blocked with) and the steps' label. It returns
  `summaryParts`, names drawn as code (`summary` keeps the plain text): "Mandu
  blocked 1 request that carried your secret `GITHUB_TOKEN` and hid your
  secret `PASTE_KEY` from the AI. 2 requests left this machine with your
  secrets `GITHUB_TOKEN` and `PASTE_KEY` filled in, each to a destination
  allowed to receive it." One request reads "…filled in, to a destination
  allowed to receive it.", never "each" (2026-10-06).
  - Each secret is named once (`distinctItems`: one name under two tokens
    reads once; an unnamed item is never merged with another).
  - *hid* names the secrets the turn's `secret` results held and counts what
    it cannot name: "hid 1 secret from the AI" (the proxy's note alone, or an
    unnamed secret), "hid your secret `A` and 1 other secret from the AI".
  - *blocked* tells each kind of block in its own words, so one kind never
    hides another's names (2026-10-07, nightly run 0930; it named only when
    every blocked step was a send that carried items, so a turn with a
    refused send and two refused reads read "Mandu blocked 3 actions"):
    the sends whose items are known are named ("blocked 1 request that
    carried your secret `GITHUB_TOKEN`"); the other blocks are counted
    ("blocked 2 actions", "blocked 1 other action" beside a named send,
    right after it); a program's refused reads of secret files (*A refused
    read is a block, not a mask* above: blocked by its note alone, no check)
    are counted as reads ("stopped 2 reads of secret files"). So the
    walkthrough's turn reads "Mandu blocked 1 request that carried your
    secret `GITHUB_TOKEN`, stopped 2 reads of secret files and hid your
    secret `PASTE_KEY` from the AI." A step a check blocked stays an action
    even when its note also refused a read (its own note is "Mandu stopped
    it."). Each kind is its own item of the line's list, never "`A` and 1
    other action" after a list of names. *sent* names only when every
    send's items are known; otherwise "a real value".
  - Each name follows from the same event as the step below it. Tone and
    order are unchanged.
  - A name comes from a file or a variable, never from a command or an
    address (*A command's output is never named by a piece of the command*
    above, 2026-10-07): a shell tool's masked output is counted ("hid 1
    secret").

  Tests: `agent-page.test.ts`, `leaves-machine.test.ts`,
  `home-js-agent.test.ts`, `session-walkthrough.test.ts`; the kinds of
  block side by side over the real components:
  `tests/stack/dashboard-refused-read.test.ts`.
- **The background line names what ran** (2026-10-05). Each turn ended with
  "Plus 4 routine checks, including connections to api.anthropic.com."
  Those four were connections, not checks, while "check" means a decision
  Mandu recorded everywhere else (§4.2f's path stop, the tool cards' check
  line). The count also lumped five kinds together, so a reader learned
  neither what ran in the background nor how Mandu took part.
  `routineParts` (`StoryTurn.routine.parts`) now names each kind of the
  paired turn's Background groups once, in a fixed order, with its count:
  "In the background: 6 connections to `api.anthropic.com`; 3 commands
  Mandu checked; 2 file paths translated between your folder and the AI's
  masked copy of it."
  - connections: "N connections to `a`, `b` and `c`", each host as code
    (three, then "and N more"; "N connections" when no host was recorded);
  - command checks: "N commands Mandu checked" (the exec guard's allowed or
    unannotated records with no tool call; a proxy's check on the agent's
    own call is that call's, whatever order the two were recorded in, §4.2f);
  - path mappings: "N file paths translated between your folder and the

  - reply checks: "N updates to your screen with the real text in place of

  - sandbox records: "N records of the sandboxed reader's work, shown

    dropped.

  The words claim nothing the groups do not hold: no "allowed" for a
  connection whose action was not recorded, and nothing about what a
  connection carried (a send that carried a secret is a step, never
  background). The line's tooltip: "Steps that needed nothing from you.
  The detailed trace lists each one." (the second sentence only with the

  (`#agent-story .routine code`). `count` and `hosts` are kept, and a
  payload without `parts` still draws "In the background: N steps."
  Tests: `agent-page.test.ts`, `home-js-agent.test.ts`,
  `session-walkthrough.test.ts` (the `background` fixture: the AI's model
  calls and an exec-supervisor record inside the turn).
- **Read as it was, masked only later** (2026-10-05). A file the AI read
  unmasked and that was labelled a secret afterwards is masked in every
  LATER request: the proxy re-masks the history `tool_result`, so the same
  call's re-send carries a token (a `symbolize` minting it, or a masked

  masked before the AI read it" and "Mandu masked 1 item", while the AI's
  reply on the same page quoted the token: the minted symbol of the re-send

  was kept from the AI at that turn), the note "The AI got this as it was:

  `<time>` on, after it was marked a secret." The summary names the
  secret as the steps do: "The AI read your secret `staging.conf` as it
  was: it was marked secret only later." (2026-10-06; it read "1 item",
  so a reader could not tell which). When a read held anything the page
  cannot name (a secret with no name, an item that is not a secret, or
  nothing recorded), it counts as before: "The AI read 1 item as it was:
  …". A moment is a `time` part (an ISO `text`), drawn by home.js
